text:
[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Random Experiments, Empirical Probability, and Frequency Stabilization",
    "scope": "Introduces the foundational motivation of probability theory as the mathematical analysis of random phenomena and uncertainty. Defines random experiments whose outcomes are not predetermined and contrasts theoretical probability with empirical (relative frequency) probability. Explains empirical frequency stabilization as trials grow from 10^2 to 10^6, detailing the convergence rate and the practical limitations of empirical estimation.",
    "key_points": [
      "Random experiment definition: an observational process whose specific outcome cannot be predetermined",
      "Empirical probability definition: P(A) ≈ (number of times A occurred) / (total trials n)",
      "Empirical frequency stabilization: as n -> infinity, relative frequency m/n stabilizes to theoretical probability p",
      "Empirical coin toss demonstration across n = 10^2, 10^4, 10^6 trials showing error reduction from 10^-1 to 10^-3",
      "Limitation of empirical probability: requires large numbers of identical, independent repeatable trials"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "Sample Spaces and Event Classification",
    "scope": "Formalizes the foundational universe of outcomes for random experiments. Distinguishes finite, countably infinite, and uncountably infinite sample spaces, showing how experiment modeling choices alter the sample space. Defines events as subsets of the sample space and classifies simple, compound, certain, and impossible (null) events.",
    "key_points": [
      "Sample space S: the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment",
      "Classification of S by cardinality: finite (coin toss {H, T}, die {1..6}), countably infinite (email arrivals {0, 1, 2, ...}), and uncountably infinite (component lifetime [0, infinity), voltage R, particle position R^3)",
      "Granularity in sample space modeling: multiple valid sample spaces exist for an experiment depending on the question (e.g., die roll top face {1..6} vs parity {even, odd})",
      "Event A as a subset A ⊆ S; occurrence criteria omega in A",
      "Simple events (singletons) vs compound events (multiple outcomes)",
      "Certain event S and impossible/null event empty set (e.g., even factors of 7, naked-eye detection of bacteria)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "Set Operations on Events and Algebraic Identities",
    "scope": "Establishes the algebraic framework translating probabilistic descriptions into formal set operations. Defines complement, intersection, union, difference, and symmetric difference, and proves foundational set identities including De Morgan's laws for finite and multiple events. Formulates mutual exclusivity (disjointness) as the absence of common outcomes.",
    "key_points": [
      "Complement A^c = {omega in S : omega not in A} (event A does not occur)",
      "Intersection A ∩ B = {omega in S : omega in A and omega in B} (both events occur)",
      "Union A ∪ B = {omega in S : omega in A or omega in B} (at least one occurs)",
      "Set difference A \\ B = A ∩ B^c (A occurs but not B)",
      "Symmetric difference A Δ B = (A \\ B) ∪ (B \\ A) = (A ∪ B) \\ (A ∩ B) (exactly one occurs)",
      "Mutually exclusive / disjoint events: A ∩ B = empty set",
      "Fundamental identities: A ∩ empty set = empty set, A ∪ empty set = A, A ∩ A^c = empty set, A ∪ A^c = S, S^c = empty set, (A^c)^c = A",
      "De Morgan's laws: (A ∩ B)^c = A^c ∪ B^c and (A ∪ B)^c = A^c ∩ B^c",
      "Generalization and element-wise membership proof of De Morgan's law: omega in (A1 ∩ A2 ∩ A3)^c <=> omega in A1^c ∪ A2^c ∪ A3^c"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "σ-Algebras and Measurable Spaces",
    "scope": "Addresses why not every arbitrary subset of an uncountable sample space can be assigned a probability, motivating the measure-theoretic concept of an event space. Defines a σ-algebra rigorously via its three defining axioms and examines the structure of generated σ-algebras on finite and infinite spaces. Investigates closure properties under intersections and provides counterexamples for unions.",
    "key_points": [
      "Motivation for σ-algebras: inability to consistently assign probabilities to all subsets of uncountable spaces (Banach-Tarski / non-measurable sets)",
      "Definition of σ-algebra F on S: S in F, closed under complement (A in F => A^c in F), closed under countable unions (A_i in F => U_{i=1}^infinity A_i in F)",
      "Measurable space (S, F) definition",
      "Reduction on finite sets: countable unions reduce to finite unions",
      "Catalog of σ-algebras: trivial {empty set, S}, power set 2^S, single-subset {empty set, A, A^c, S}, Borel σ-algebra B(R) generated by open intervals, and countable-cocountable σ-algebra",
      "Atoms of a partition: the σ-algebra generated by a partition of n atoms contains exactly 2^n elements",
      "Theorem: the intersection of two σ-algebras F1 ∩ F2 is always a σ-algebra (proof)",
      "Counterexample: the union F1 ∪ F2 is generally not a σ-algebra due to failure of union closure"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "The Kolmogorov Axioms of Probability",
    "scope": "Introduces Kolmogorov's axiomatic foundation of modern probability theory. Defines a probability measure on a measurable space, formalizing the three core axioms: Non-negativity, Normalization, and Countable Additivity. Contrasts valid probability measures with pathological or invalid candidate assignments on finite and countably infinite spaces.",
    "key_points": [
      "Probability measure P: F -> [0, 1] (or R) and the probability space triple (S, F, P)",
      "Axiom 1 (Non-negativity): P(A) >= 0 for all A in F",
      "Axiom 2 (Normalization): P(S) = 1",
      "Axiom 3 (Countable Additivity): for pairwise disjoint events A_1, A_2, ..., P(U_{i=1}^infinity A_i) = sum_{i=1}^infinity P(A_i)",
      "Verification of axioms on discrete spaces: sum of outcome weights must equal 1 and each weight >= 0",
      "Non-examples: negative weights violating non-negativity, total mass != 1 violating normalization, non-linear functions (e.g., (|A|/n)^2) violating additivity",
      "Pathology on infinite sets: the finite/infinite measure Q(A) = 0 (finite) or 1 (infinite) fails both finite additivity and countable additivity"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "Fundamental Theorems and Properties Derived from the Axioms",
    "scope": "Develops the rigorous deductive machinery of probability by deriving all core operational rules directly from the Kolmogorov axioms. Proves the probability of the empty set, the complement rule, finite additivity, and monotonicity. Establishes the probability formula for set differences and states Boole's inequality (the union bound).",
    "key_points": [
      "Theorem: P(empty set) = 0 (proof via disjoint union S = S ∪ empty set and Axiom 3)",
      "Finite additivity: P(U_{i=1}^n A_i) = sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i) for pairwise disjoint A_i",
      "Complement rule: P(A^c) = 1 - P(A) (proof via S = A ∪ A^c and Axiom 2)",
      "Monotonicity: if A ⊆ B, then P(A) <= P(B) (proof via decomposition B = A ∪ (B \\ A) and Non-negativity)",
      "Set difference rule: P(B \\ A) = P(B) - P(A) whenever A ⊆ B, and P(A \\ B) = P(A) - P(A ∩ B) in general",
      "Union bound (Boole's inequality): P(U_{i=1}^n A_i) <= sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "Addition Rules and the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion",
    "scope": "Extends probability evaluation to overlapping (non-disjoint) events. Proves the addition rule for two events by resolving double-counting and derives the mutually exclusive special case. Formulates and applies the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for three events, systematically deducing probabilities of complex compound events including at least one, at least two, and exactly one occurrence.",
    "key_points": [
      "Theorem (Addition Rule for Two Events): P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B) (proof by partitioning into disjoint components)",
      "Corollary for disjoint events: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)",
      "Theorem (Inclusion-Exclusion for Three Events): P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(A ∩ B) - P(A ∩ C) - P(B ∩ C) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C)",
      "Probability of 'at least two of three': sum_{i<j} P(A_i ∩ A_j) - 2*P(A ∩ B ∩ C)",
      "Probability of 'exactly one of three': P(A ∪ B ∪ C) - P('at least two')",
      "Probability of 'none': P(A^c ∩ B^c ∩ C^c) = 1 - P(A ∪ B ∪ C)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "Classical Probability and Discrete Weight Assignments",
    "scope": "Covers probability models for finite and countably infinite sample spaces where probabilities are assigned to individual points. Develops the classical Laplace probability model under the assumption of equally likely outcomes using combinatorial counting. Explores non-uniform discrete weight distributions on finite and countably infinite spaces, including loaded dice and geometric series normalization.",
    "key_points": [
      "Discrete probability: P(A) = sum_{omega in A} P({omega}) where weights satisfy P({omega}) >= 0 and sum_{omega in S} P({omega}) = 1",
      "Classical (Laplace) model: S has N equally likely outcomes, each with weight 1/N; P(A) = |A| / |S| = m / N",
      "Combinatorial applications: sampling without replacement using binomial coefficients (hypergeometric forms (C(K, k)*C(N-K, n-k))/C(N, n))",
      "Weighted discrete spaces: loaded die modeling with linear constraints (even faces twice as likely as odd faces)",
      "Countably infinite probability measures: geometric series distribution P({k}) = c / 3^k, solving for normalization constant c = 2, and evaluating tail/parity probabilities"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 9,
    "title": "Geometric Probability",
    "scope": "Extends probability from discrete counting to continuous sample spaces embedded in Euclidean space R^n where individual points have zero probability. Defines geometric probability as the ratio of Lebesgue measures (length, area, volume). Solves canonical continuous problems including the two-person meeting problem and the broken stick problem for triangle formation.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: P(A) = measure(A) / measure(S) where measure represents length in R, area in R^2, or volume in R^3 for uniformly distributed continuous outcomes",
      "The Meeting Problem: independent uniform arrivals x, y in [0, 60] with sample space area 3600",
      "Meeting region formulation: |x - y| <= t represented by the strip x - t <= y <= x + t",
      "Complementary area method: computing non-meeting area via two corner right triangles of leg (60 - t) to find P(meeting) = 1 - ((60 - t)/60)^2",
      "Inverse meeting threshold: solving for waiting time t needed to guarantee P(meeting) >= 1/2 (t >= 60 - 30*sqrt(2) ≈ 17.57 min)",
      "The Broken Stick Problem: breaking [0, 1] at two uniform points x, y to form a triangle",
      "Triangle inequality reduction: three pieces form a triangle iff every piece is shorter than 1/2, yielding successful area 1/4 (sum of two 1/8 triangles)"
    ]
  }
]
